paper_title: PAIR: Bridging Perception and Action in Vision-Language-Action Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to continuous robot actions. This task requires a transition from representations that describe the scene and instruction to representations that support action generation. Many continuous-action VLAs leave this transition implicit and supervise it mainly through the final action-prediction loss. We introduce PAIR, a framework that learns a shared perception-action representation between these two spaces. During training, a Masked Action Autoencoder encodes expert action chunks into horizon-aligned Action Latent Tokens. A Bridge Module extracts task-relevant features from the current visual-language representations. PAIR aligns these features with the Action Latent Tokens to form Bridge Tokens that preserve task information and capture the structure of expert actions. The Bridge Tokens are then projected into the action-token space and injected into the initial Action Tokens, providing an action-ready starting point for Action Expert refinement. At inference, the autoencoder is removed, and the Bridge Tokens are generated only from the current observation and instruction. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and CALVIN ABC-D show gains for the evaluated OpenVLA-OFT and VLA-Adapter models. On LIBERO-Plus, PAIR raises VLA-Adapter's success rate from 59.1% to 64.2%. On CALVIN, it increases VLA-Adapter's average completed sequence length from 4.42 to 4.53. Across seven real-world tasks, PAIR raises OpenVLA-OFT's success rate from 51.4% to 65.0%. Representation analyses show that Bridge Tokens retain task information while making continuous-action information accessible before Action Expert refinement. These results support a shared intermediate representation as a useful interface between perception and action in continuous-action VLAs.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have emerged as promising framework for robot control. By mapping visual observations and language instructions to continuous actions, they unify visual grounding, language understanding, and control within single policy. Recent models have achieved strong performance across diverse manipulation tasks (Brohan et al., 2022; 2023; Kim et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2026). Yet this unified formulation hides difficult representational transition. The visual-language perception space and the action space are organized around fundamentally different semantics. The former describes the current world and the intended task, including scene content, object relations, and instruction-level intent. The latter specifies how the robot should act through temporally ordered, executable control. We refer to this semantic mismatch as the perceptionaction representation gap. Existing VLA policies learn to traverse this gap primarily through end-to-end action supervision. The final action loss specifies which action should be produced, while the representation that connects visual-language semantics to action semantics is left implicit. Action tokens must therefore discover within the policy both what information is relevant to control and how it should be reorganized into an action-ready representation. Recent work has sought to facilitate this transition by exposing control-relevant structure through visual traces, affordances, visual reasoning, and learned latent actions (Zheng et al., 2025; Nasiriany et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026b). These efforts show that making such structure 1 Figure 1: Conceptual view of the perception-to-action transition. Standard VLAs require Action Tokens to acquire and organize action-relevant information during decoding. PAIR instead learns perception-derived Bridge Tokens shaped by the structure of expert actions and injects them into the initial Action Tokens, so that the Action Expert begins from an action-ready intermediate state and refines it toward continuous control. The Action Autoencoder is used only during training. explicit can facilitate action generation. Yet robot demonstrations already pair the two sides of the transition: visuallanguage context specifies what behavior is required, while expert actions reveal how that behavior is executed. This raises central question: Can we learn the missing intermediate representation directly from perception and actiona bridge that carries task semantics from one space and executable structure from the other? We introduce PAIR, framework for learning PerceptionAction Intermediate Representation directly from paired robot demonstrations. From the action side, Masked Action Autoencoder encodes expert action chunks into Action Latent Tokens. Reconstructing the demonstrated actions requires these tokens to preserve the temporal and executable structure. From the perception side, Bridge Module condenses the current visual-language representations into compact, task-relevant features. Aligning these features with the Action Latent Tokens transfers action structure into the perception-derived representation, forming Bridge Tokens that jointly encode task semantics and action information. Perception supplies the semantic content, expert actions supply the executable structure, and alignment integrates both into unified bridge. PAIR then projects the Bridge Tokens into the action-token space and injects them at the beginning of action decoding. This early Bridge Injection primes the action tokens with task-aware and action-structured information, providing an explicit starting point for the perception-to-action transition. The policy can then refine this prior through its original action-decoding process rather than constructing an action-ready representation from the final action objective alone. Experiments on LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023), LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2026), and CALVIN ABCD (Mees et al., 2022) demonstrate consistent gains across OpenVLA-OFT and VLA-Adapter. PAIR raises the average success rate of VLA-Adapter from 97.3% to 98.4% on LIBERO and from 59.1% to 64.2% on LIBERO-Plus. On CALVIN, it improves the average completed sequence length from 4.28 to 4.40 with OpenVLA-OFT and from 4.42 to 4.53 with VLA-Adapter. Across seven realworld tasks, PAIR further raises the average success rate of OpenVLA-OFT from 51.4% to 65.0%. These improvements span standard manipulation, zero-shot distribution shifts and long-horizon execution. Representation analyses further show that Bridge Tokens retain task context while exposing action structure before decoding, supporting their role as an explicit interface between perception and action. Contributions. Our contributions are as follows: We characterize the perceptionaction representation gap in continuous-action VLAs as the implicit transition from visuallanguage semantics to executable action semantics under final action supervision. 2 We introduce PAIR, which learns perception-derived Bridge Tokens whose task semantics are organized by expert-action structure, and uses early Bridge Injection to provide Action Tokens with an action-aware starting point for refinement. We demonstrate consistent gains across standard manipulation, zero-shot distribution shifts, long-horizon execution, and real-world control, together with representation-level evidence that Bridge Tokens retain task semantics while exposing action structure before Action Expert refinement.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Intermediate representations for perception-to-action learning. Intermediate representations make control-relevant structure explicit before action prediction. Motion-oriented approaches encode trajectories, visual traces, or future scene changes (Niu et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). Spatial representations introduce geometric information into perception and action modeling (Qu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025), while affordance-based methods describe possible interactions or key robot configurations (Nasiriany et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2026). These approaches define the intermediate representation through chosen physical abstraction, such as motion, geometry, or affordance. PAIR does not prescribe particular physical meaning for the bridge. Its content is learned from the two spaces it is meant to connect: visuallanguage context provides task semantics, while expert actions organize the representation around executable structure. In this way, task context and action structure jointly determine what the intermediate representation retains. Latent action representations and tokenization. Latent action methods learn compact representations of robot behavior for pretraining, prediction, and control. LAPA derives discrete latent actions from visual transitions for VLA pretraining without robot action labels (Ye et al., 2025), while UniVLA learns task-centric latent actions for policy learning (Bu et al., 2025). FAST and VQ-VLA tokenize continuous action chunks for token-based policies (Pertsch et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a). These approaches primarily structure how actions themselves are represented, tokenized, or predicted. LARA (Liu et al., 2026b) moves closer to the perceptionaction interface by aligning latent visual dynamics with intermediate Action Expert features during generation. PAIR targets different object: perception-derived intermediate representation that is shaped by expertaction structure during training and made available before Action Expert refinement begins.

sections.title: 3.3 BRIDGE INJECTION
sections.content: Bridge Tokens are learned to mediate the transition from visuallanguage semantics to executable action. We place them at the beginning of the Action Expert, where Action Tokens enter the computation that develops their action semantics. This early injection primes the Action Tokens with the information represented on both sides of the transition. Because task-relevant context and action structure are available from the first expert block, the Action Tokens begin from an explicit intermediate state and refine it toward executable control. 3.4 TRAINING The two training stages follow the construction of the intermediate representation. The first stage learns action structure by optimizing the Masked Action Autoencoder with LAE. The second stage freezes the autoencoder and transfers this structure to the perception-derived Bridge Tokens while learning to use them inside the policy. Let Lact denote the original continuous action prediction loss of the VLA policy. The second-stage objective is LPAIR = Lact + λalignLalign, (6) where λalign controls the contribution of the representation alignment objective. The VLA policy and bridge module are optimized jointly in this stage. During inference, the Bridge Module extracts Bridge Tokens from the current visuallanguage representations. Bridge Injection then primes the Action Tokens at the beginning of the Action Expert for continuous action prediction.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: Our experiments address three questions: Does PAIR improve manipulation performance, zero-shot generalization, and long-horizon execution, and do these gains extend to real-world tasks? (Secs. 4.24.3) Do Bridge Tokens encode task semantics and action structure before the Action Expert, and how does their action information compare with baseline Action Tokens across layers? (Section 4.4) How do action alignment and injection position affect PAIRs performance, and what are the contributions of adaptive injection and autoencoder noise? (Section 4.5; Appendix A)

sections.title: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Benchmarks and metrics. LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) evaluates task-conditioned manipulation across the Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long suites, which vary spatial relationships, manipulated objects, task goals, and action-sequence length. We evaluate each task over 50 rollouts from the official initial states and report success rates for each suite and their average. Following the official protocol, LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2026) evaluates the corresponding LIBERO-trained checkpoints zero-shot under changes in camera viewpoint, robot initial state, language instruction, lighting, background, sensor noise, and object layout. CALVIN ABCD (Mees et al., 2022) trains policies in environments AC and evaluates 1,000 five-task chains in unseen environment D. We report success at completing at least one to five consecutive tasks and average completed sequence length, capturing both individual-task performance and sustained execution. Additional protocols are in Appendix C. Backbones and implementation. We evaluate PAIR with VLA-Adapter (Wang et al., 2026) on LIBERO/Plus, both VLA-Adapter and OpenVLA-OFT (Kim et al., 2025a) on CALVIN, and OpenVLA-OFT on the real robot. Each + PAIR row augments the preceding backbone. We train on four NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada Generation GPUs; detailed training settings are provided in Appendix C. 4.2 SIMULATION RESULTS We report PAIRs aggregate results as mean standard deviation over three random seeds. Platform and tasks. We evaluate seven tasks on UFACTORY UF850 with synchronized thirdperson and wrist-mounted Intel RealSense RGB observations and robot proprioception (Figure 3). Object placement, cube placement, and cup stacking require selecting or arranging objects according to the instruction; button pressing requires executing specified color order. Board wiping involves sustained tool contact, water pouring requires controlled liquid transfer, and drawer loading combines opening the specified drawer with placing bowl inside. Together, these tasks cover 7 language-conditioned selection, sequential interaction, precise placement, and contact-rich manipulation. Task instructions and demonstration sequences are provided in Appendix C.3. Demonstration data and evaluation. We collect expert demonstrations through Quest VR teleoperation, with 3051 trajectories per task and 293 trajectories in total. OpenVLA-OFT and PAIR use identical processed demonstrations and train separate policy for each task. Each method is evaluated over 20 trials per task, totaling 140 trials across the seven tasks. Results. PAIR improves OpenVLA-OFT on all seven tasks, from 51.4% to 65.0% overall (Figure 4). Gains span object placement (+15 points), sequential button pressing (+5), and drawer loading (+15), with the largest gain in water pouring (+20). Improvements therefore appear in both instruction-driven discrete interactions and tasks requiring extended control over object motion or contact, extending the simulation results to physical manipulation. Figure 4: Real-world success rates over 20 trials per task. PAIR improves OpenVLA-OFT across all seven tasks, with an overall gain of 13.6 percentage points. 4.4 ANALYSIS Using frozen representations from 500 task-balanced LIBERO-Spatial frames, Figure 5(a) uses fivefold linear probes with trajectory-grouped splits to predict ten task identities and eight coarse action modes clustered from ground-truth action chunks. sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: PAIR introduces an explicit intermediate representation for the perception-to-action transition in continuous-action VLAs. Bridge Tokens combine visuallanguage context with action structure and prime Action Tokens at the entrance of the Action Expert. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, and seven real-world tasks, PAIR improves two VLA backbones in standard manipulation, zero-shot generalization, long-horizon execution, and physical control. Representation analyses show that the learned bridge carries both task and action information, while ablations identify action alignment and early injection as its key ingredients. These results establish explicit perception action intermediates as practical design principle for VLA policies.

sections.title: B ADDITIONAL ANALYSIS
sections.content: B.1 LAYERWISE PROBE PROTOCOL For the layerwise analysis in Figure 6, we use frozen representations from LIBERO-Spatial, with 500 training-set frames balanced across the ten tasks. Each example contains eight pre-LLM Bridge Tokens, the corresponding Action Latent Tokens, and an eight-step, seven-dimensional ground-truth action chunk. Both the BridgeAction Latent and Bridgebaseline Action Token comparisons use the same 500 frames, action targets, and trajectory-grouped folds. Baseline VLA-Adapter Action Tokens are extracted before the Transformer and after each of its 24 blocks. Classification and regression. Representations are flattened, standardized, and reduced to 50 principal components when their input dimension exceeds 128. Preprocessing is fit on the training portion of each fold. Task classification uses the ten task identities; action classification uses eight KMeans clusters of standardized ground-truth action chunks (K = 8, 20 initializations, seed 7). multinomial logistic-regression probe with = 1 is evaluated using five trajectory-grouped folds, with all frames from each trajectory assigned to the same fold. We report mean balanced accuracy and fold standard deviation. Continuous-action prediction uses ridge regression (α = 10) on the same trajectory-grouped folds with training-fold target standardization; we report varianceweighted R2. The split seed is 7. 12 B.2 TASK AND ACTION INFORMATION ACROSS DEPTH Figure 6: Task identity and action-cluster decodability across depth. Blue curves show baseline Action Tokens with fold-standard-deviation bands. Green dashed lines indicate the pre-LLM Bridge Token score. Layer 0 precedes the Transformer; layers 124 denote completed blocks. Figure 6 separates access to task identity from access to action patterns. Baseline Action Tokens acquire task information rapidly: task accuracy reaches 97.0% after the first block and remains high through much of the network, ending at 89.6%. Their action-cluster accuracy develops more gradually and reaches 89.1% at the final block. Bridge Tokens provide 87.8% task accuracy together with 91.5% action-cluster accuracy before entering the Action Expert, making both forms of information accessible from the beginning of action generation. Depth-wise transition. The two baseline curves evolve differently: task identity becomes accessible after the first block, whereas action-cluster structure accumulates more gradually. The Bridge Token operating point combines both signals before any Action Expert block. Its task accuracy remains close to the baselines late-layer level, while its action-cluster accuracy already exceeds the final baseline value. This pattern complements the entrance-injection ablation: PAIR makes an action-aware state available at the start of refinement, while the baseline develops action structure across later blocks. B.3 CONTINUOUS-ACTION DECODING ACROSS DEPTH Figure 7 directly compares how much continuous control information is readable from the two Action-Token pathways. After Bridge Token injection, PAIR begins at 47.3% decoding score, compared with 20.1% for the baseline tokens before the Transformer. The advantage is largest at the entrance, remains visible across most early and middle depths, and reappears at the final block (76.4% versus 72.7%). Thus, the injected Action Tokens start from more action-readable state and retain that advantage through refinement. 13 Figure 7: Continuous-action decodability of Action Tokens across depth. Ridge readouts predict the full eight-step ground-truth action chunk from frozen Action Tokens. Scores are 1 MAE after target normalization, pooled over five trajectory-grouped held-out folds on 1,000 shared LIBEROSpatial examples. PAIR tokens are measured after Bridge Token injection; baseline tokens are measured before and after each Transformer block. B.4 ADDITIONAL ACTION-GEOMETRY EVIDENCE Figure 8: Action-cluster geometry and kernel alignment. (a,b) Cosine similarities between GTderived action-cluster centroids in the two spaces, using shared color scale. A0A7 index unsupervised clusters rather than named behaviors. (c) Within-task linear CKA. Error bars indicate task standard deviation for Bridge Tokens and the 5th95th percentile interval of the trajectorypermutation reference. Sampling and comparison. The geometry analysis uses separate deterministic 500-frame subset: two ordered frames from each of 25 trajectories per task. Bridge representations and groundtruth actions are independently flattened, feature-wise standardized, centered within each task, and L2-normalized. RSA compares cosine-distance ranks for same-task, cross-trajectory pairs. Top-10 neighbor overlap uses the same task and trajectory restrictions. Linear CKA compares the centered cosine Gram matrices within each task. Scores are averaged across the ten tasks. The permutation reference reassigns complete two-frame trajectory groups within each task 200 times while retaining their internal order. 14 Action geometry across complementary metrics. The centroid heatmaps summarize relationships among action-cluster means. Positive similarity between A0 and A1 and between A3 and A5, and negative similarity between A2 and A3, are retained across the two spaces. Differences between the matrices reflect the perceptual and task context carried by Bridge Tokens. At the sample level, linear CKA reaches 0.887 compared with 0.148 under shuffled correspondence, with task-wise values ranging from 0.865 to 0.909. Together with the distance-ranking and neighborhood results in the main text, these metrics show action structure at both sample and cluster levels.

sections.title: C IMPLEMENTATION AND EVALUATION DETAILS
sections.content: C.1 TRAINING HYPERPARAMETERS Table 9: Default training hyperparameters. Batch denotes the effective batch size across four GPUs. The OpenVLA-OFT learning rate remains constant because its decay milestone follows the 50k-step run. Stage / backbone Batch Steps Learning rate Schedule LoRA rank Action Autoencoder VLA-Adapter + PAIR OpenVLA-OFT + PAIR 64 64 64 50k 150k 50k 3104 2104 5104 cosine, 1k warmup cosine constant 64 Additional settings. The Action Autoencoder is trained for 50k steps on LIBERO demonstrations for LIBERO and zero-shot LIBERO-Plus, on CALVIN demonstrations for CALVIN, and separately on each tasks demonstrations for the seven real-world tasks. We use AdamW for both stages. The Action Autoencoder uses weight decay 104 and clips the gradient norm at 1.0. Policy training uses bfloat16, image augmentation, and alignment weight λalign = 0.1. PAIR architecture. The Action Autoencoder comprises two-layer pre-norm Transformer encoder and one-layer pre-norm Transformer decoder, both using self-attention over the action chunk with four attention heads. During training, action steps are randomly masked with probability 0.5 and Gaussian noise with standard deviation 0.05 is added before reconstruction. Both OpenVLAOFT and VLA-Adapter use eight Bridge Tokens, matching the eight action-step tokens at the input to their final Action Experts. The Bridge Module forms them from learned horizon-aligned queries using one pre-norm cross-attention block over the visuallanguage tokens, followed by one pre-norm self-attention block; both use eight attention heads and residual MLP blocks. The alignment and injection projections are two-layer MLPs with GELU activations. Injection is scaled by zero-initialized per-token gate implemented by layer normalization, scalar linear projection, and tanh nonlinearity. C.2 SIMULATION BENCHMARKS LIBERO. The Action Autoencoder is trained on LIBERO data, and the VLA-Adapter policy is trained on the corresponding suite. LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) evaluates task-conditioned manipulation across the Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long suites. These suites vary spatial relationships, manipulated objects, task goals, and the length of the required action sequence. We evaluate each task for 50 rollouts from the official initial states using 256256 environment observations, and report each suites success rate and their average. LIBERO-Plus. Following the official evaluation protocol (Fei et al., 2026), we directly evaluate the corresponding LIBERO-trained checkpoints zero-shot. The seven perturbation categories cover camera viewpoint, robot initial state, language instruction, lighting, background, sensor noise, and object layout. Per-category and overall success assess generalization beyond the original training conditions. CALVIN. We use the ABCD split (Mees et al., 2022): policies train in environments AC and execute 1,000 five-task chains in unseen environment D. OpenVLA-OFT executes each eight-step 15 action chunk open-loop before replanning. We report success at completing at least one to five consecutive tasks and average completed sequence length, measuring both individual-task performance and sustained execution. C.3 REAL-WORLD TASKS AND EVALUATION Platform, data, and evaluation. All physical experiments use UFACTORY UF850 arm with synchronized wrist-mounted and fixed third-person Intel RealSense RGB cameras. The policy receives both RGB views and robot proprioception. Expert demonstrations are collected through Quest VR teleoperation and converted to RLDS. For each task, we train separate Action Autoencoder for PAIR and separate policies for OpenVLA-OFT and PAIR on identical processed trajectories. We evaluate 20 trials per task (140 in total) and report the macro-average across the seven tasks. Table 10: Real-world task definitions and dataset sizes. The task suite spans instruction-conditioned target selection in object and cube placement, relative object reasoning and terminal alignment in cup stacking, ordered execution in button pressing, and contact-rich or articulated manipulation in board wiping, water pouring, and drawer loading.
